extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political economy, and modern British political history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating the conceptual criteria the author uses to diagnose the exhaustion of hegemonic consent and the transition from cultural dissent to state coercion in Britain c.1960s–1970s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police repression as catalyst for politicisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The police, by closing down and repressing counter-cultural activities, could convert the Underground into an active political resistance movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1969 police closures of informal street occupation brought the counter-culture up against 'the Fuzz' and helped politicise previously cultural movements. The text argues that one agency of state repression (the police) 'almost succeeded in converting the Underground into an active political resistance movement.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacular occupations as partial politicisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Planned public spectacles (e.g. squats) that deliberately assemble different tributaries of the counter-culture function as acts of partial politicisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 144 Piccadilly Squat by the London Street Commune was an 'improvisation' designed to bring together quasi-anarchists, hippies, working-class layabouts, Hell's Angels, etc.; its spectacle was 'calculated to scandalise' and to politicise disparate groups, though outcomes could be mixed (skinheads sided with police).

rubrics_metrics.name: Backlash mobilised by moral entrepreneurs and the 'silent majority'
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns by moral entrepreneurs (e.g., to 'clean up' Britain) rally a 'silent majority' and push policing and legal action against counter-cultural forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links moral campaigns (BBC clean-up, obscenity/drug enforcement) to increased police activity and a broader social backlash that constrains the counter-culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to understand target society as weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement's inability to comprehend the nature and vulnerabilities of the society it aims to subvert undermines its capacity to sustain political resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue the counter-culture 'did not itself fully understand the nature of the society it aimed to subvert, or its vulnerability', which contributed to the mirage that 'straight society' might abandon the struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment into organised left as sign of politicisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant recruitment from the counter-culture into revolutionary left groups indicates a shift from cultural dissent toward organised political struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include conversion of some counter-cultural members into International Socialists, International Marxist Group, anarchists, Solidarity, Maoist fractions—presented as evidence of partial politicisation and fusion with political militancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion, theoretical clarity, and tactical perspective as preconditions for political crystallisation
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement lacking organisational cohesion, theoretical clarity, and tactical perspective is unlikely to crystallise into a sustained autonomous political force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text diagnoses the counter-culture as 'lacking cohesion, theoretical clarity or tactical perspective'—a key reason it failed to crystallize politically despite appearing threatening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social composition of movement (new intelligentsia) as explanatory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The class origins and occupational trajectory of movement participants (predominantly middle-class/new intelligentsia) shape the character and limits of the counter-culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors describe bearers of the counter-culture as often from middle-class backgrounds, first-generation grammar/comprehensive or art school attendees—potential recruits to a 'new organic intelligentsia' whose position conditions their political role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting institutions that manufacture consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of the counter-cultural critique is judged by whether it attacks and localises assaults on institutions that produce and reproduce dominant ideology (family, media, universities, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted list: 'Women, Hippies, youth groups, students and school children all question the institutions that have formed them,' aiming to replace bourgeois family with communes, create counter-media, anti-universities—attacks must be 'specified, localized and relevant' to bring contradictions into view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-definition of liberal tolerance as 'repressive tolerance'
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement's ideological stance includes renaming liberal pluralism/tolerance as a form of repression—this reframing is a criterion for its critical posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: the counter-culture 'redefined this liberalism, this tolerance, this pluralism, this consensus, as repressive' and called 'consensus' coercive and 'freedom' domination—this reframing helps explain its oppositional logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillation between opposition and incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement's oscillation between total opposition and incorporation indicates susceptibility to containment/co-optation and undermines lasting autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note the underground 'oscillated so rapidly between extremes: total 'opposition', and incorporation,' suggesting a dialectic that often led to containment by dominant structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible re-entry of working-class struggle as watershed
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-emergence of visible, organised working-class militancy (class struggle) marks a decisive turning point that transforms cultural crisis into a state-level crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The year 1970 is described as a watershed when 'the class struggle comes more and more into the open'—this shift concentrates ruling-class attention and changes political dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of mechanisms of consent and shift to coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators that the hegemonic order is moving from consent to coercion include ritualized appeals to 'the nation', increased police measures, legal regulation, and a visible recourse to force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that when appeals to 'the nation' become invocations rather than reflections of consensus, and when state action resorts to police measures, law, and rumoured conspiracies, hegemony is exhausted and repressive closure ensues (e.g., Heath as 'Bonaparte').

rubrics_metrics.name: Recomposition of the capitalist state and its enmeshing of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: The recomposition of the state is judged by its increasing role in supervising, controlling, and integrating civil society across public and private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors describe the emerging 'augmented state' that 'enmeshes, controls, regulates, superintends and tutors civil society'—this institutional recomposition is a central mechanism in moving from consent to control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic structural weakness as root cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicators of long-term economic decline (falling export share, low investment and growth) form the structural base precipitating political crisis and the need for stronger state measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/numbers: Britain's share of world manufactured exports halved (1954–1970); investment/GNP low (16–18% vs. Japan 30–35%); growth rates much lower—these data are used to locate the structural crisis underpinning political shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage growth and wage militancy as disciplining pivot
rubrics_metrics.description: Rising wages and wage militancy are seen by capital as weakening competitiveness and become the focal point around which disciplining strategies (planning, incomes policy, legal regulation) are organised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text traces stages: capitalist planning → incomes policy → statutory/legal control; pays particular attention to the 'operator' of wage restraint as central to mounting the offensive against organised labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of corporate management on tripartite agreements and implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful corporate management strategy depends on governments, producer groups, and implementing institutions being able and willing to reach and execute agreements; failure undermines voluntary constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Professor Beer: corporate management 'depends on governments and producer groups being able to reach agreements and then on each group being able and willing to implement its part of the bargain.' NEDDY and TUC participation are used as case evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of containment: conversion to planning and exhaustion of voluntary constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of disciplining labour and civil society proceeds through identifiable phases (indicative planning, NEDDY, incomes policy, legal regulation) marking progressive exhaustion of voluntary consent mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text outlines historical sequence: early 'conversion to planning' after 1956–57, NEDDY and TUC involvement, Wilson's two-faced interventionism, then Heath's more overt legal/regulatory instruments—these stages are diagnostic markers of containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of ideological/mental production apparatuses as material base of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth and coordination of media, education, science and technique (the 'consciousness-making industries' and 'social brain') are essential material supports for ideological reproduction and thus for attempts to sustain consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that these industries are tied to new technologies and the 'third industrial revolution' and were massively expanded and superintended by the state; their expansion is both material and ideological support for hegemony.
